OF THOMAS MORE’S UTOPIA

it is not of royal dignity to exercise authority over beggars, but rather over the wealthy and happy. Fabricius, a man of upright and lofty character, certainly perceived this himself when he replied that he would rather rule over rich men than be rich himself. And indeed, for one man to flow with pleasure and luxuries while others groan and lament on every side is not to be the custodian of a kingdom, but of a prison. Finally, just as the most unskilled doctor is one who knows not how to cure a disease except by another disease, so too is he who knows not how to correct the lives of citizens except by removing the comforts of life; let him admit that he does not know how to rule over free men. Rather, let him cast off his own sloth or arrogance, for it is usually because of these vices that a people either despises him or holds him in hatred. Let him live harmlessly on his own means, let him adjust his expenses to his income, let him restrain crimes, and by the proper instruction of his subjects, let him prevent them from growing rather than allow them to increase only to punish them later. Let him not recklessly recall laws abrogated by custom, especially those that have long been forgotten and have never been missed. And let him never seize anything under the pretext of an offense that a judge would not allow a private citizen to accept, as it would be considered unjust and crafty. Here, if I were to propose to them the law of the Macarenses, who themselves are not far removed from Utopia, whose king, on the very day he begins his reign, is bound by an oath after great sacrifices that he will never have more than a thousand pounds of gold in his treasury, or an amount of silver equal to the value of that gold. They say this law was established by a certain excellent king, for whom the advantage of his country was of greater concern than
<margin>A wonderful law of the Macarenses</margin>

<summary>This page argues that a true king secures his authority through the welfare and prosperity of his subjects rather than through their impoverishment. It concludes with the example of the Macarenses, who legally limit the royal treasury to prevent the hoarding of wealth at the expense of the state.</summary>
